clinicalPearls: The cardinal features are colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distention, emesis, and obstipation; distal obstruction tends to produce more distention and later, sometimes feculent, vomiting, whereas proximal obstruction produces more pronounced vomiting with less distention (Harrison 22e p.2591).

Obstruction is characterized as partial, high grade, or complete, which generally tracks with the risk of complications and the urgency of intervention; it is termed simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia are present (Harrison 22e p.2589).

Roughly 80% of cases involve the small bowel, and about one-third of small-bowel cases show significant ischemia; obstruction accounts for about 1-3% of hospitalizations and a quarter of urgent/emergent general surgery admissions (Harrison 22e p.2589).

Postoperative adhesions are the single most common cause (>50% overall), followed by neoplasms (~20%) and hernias (~10%); lower abdominal operations (appendectomy, colorectal, gynecologic) are especially adhesiogenic (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

Classic early small-bowel obstruction produces high-pitched 'musical' tinkling bowel sounds and peristaltic rushes (borborygmi), which later become absent or hypoactive; in ileus/pseudo-obstruction sounds are typically absent or hypoactive from the start (Harrison 22e p.2591).
A tender abdominal or groin mass strongly suggests an incarcerated hernia; pain out of proportion to physical findings can mimic acute mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591).

Carcinomatosis causing obstruction most often originates from the ovary, but can arise from the pancreas, stomach, or colon, and rarely from distant sites such as breast or skin (Harrison 22e p.2589).

In adult intussusception the lead point is typically a polyp or tumor; in gallstone 'ileus' the most common obstruction site is the ileum (~60%), with the stone usually entering via a cholecystoduodenal fistula (Harrison 22e p.2590, 2593).

Sigmoid colon volvulus comprises about two-thirds of all volvulus cases and ~4% of large-bowel obstruction; risk factors include institutionalization, neuropsychiatric conditions on psychotropics, chronic constipation, and advanced age (seventies-eighties) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

Stasis raises bacterial counts in the jejunum and ileum; organisms such as Escherichia coli, Streptococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella may be recovered from intestinal cultures, mesenteric nodes, and blood (Harrison 22e p.2590).

CT is the most frequently used modality, with sensitivity ~95% (78-100%) and specificity ~96% for high-grade obstruction, but accuracy for closed-loop obstruction is much lower (~60%) (Harrison 22e p.2592).
Contrast appearing within the cecum 4-24 h after oral water-soluble contrast predicts improvement with high (~95%) sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.2592).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute obstruction is either mechanical (extrinsic, intrinsic bowel-wall, or intraluminal lesions) or functional (dysmotility without blockage). Increased contractility proximal and distal to the block is characteristic; peristalsis then slows as proximal bowel dilates and fills with secretions and swallowed air, with additional luminal gas from fermentation and CO2 production. Rising intraluminal pressure exceeding venous pressure impairs venous and lymphatic drainage, producing wall edema and proximal hypoxemia, with epithelial necrosis identifiable within 12 h. Progressive arterial compromise can cause full-thickness ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Inflammatory edema generates reactive oxygen species and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, disrupting secretory and neuromotor function. Loss of absorptive capacity plus fluid sequestration in the bowel wall and peritoneum causes dehydration; anorexia and emesis worsen volume depletion, and high-grade distal obstruction with vomiting causes loss of gastric potassium, hydrogen, and chloride while dehydration drives proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption (metabolic alkalosis). Closed-loop obstruction, in which both ends of a segment are occluded (e.g., volvulus, hernia), is the most common precursor to strangulation and carries high risk of vascular insufficiency and irreversible ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2590-2591).
additionalDifferentials: Postoperative ileus (functional obstruction following intraabdominal surgery)
Obstructive colon cancer (may mimic small-bowel obstruction when the ileocecal valve is incompetent)
Crohn's disease and other inflammatory strictures
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to findings)
nonInfectiousMimics: Adynamic ileus from metabolic/electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, uremia, severe hyperglycemia)
Drug-induced dysmotility (opiates, antihistamines, anticholinergics, some psychotropics)
Intestinal ischemia presenting with functional dysmotility
Collagen vascular disease (e.g., lupus, scleroderma) causing visceral dysmotility
additionalInvestigations: Complete blood count and serum electrolytes/creatinine with serial assessment (mild hemoconcentration and slight leukocytosis are common in simple obstruction)
Upright/cross-table lateral abdominal radiographs ('staircasing' of dilated small-bowel loops >2.5 cm, air-fluid levels, 'coffee bean' shadow in volvulus)
CT with enteral and IV contrast (location, closed-loop, and ischemia features such as altered wall enhancement, mesenteric venous gas, pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum)
Markers possibly suggestive of strangulation: serum D-lactate, creatine kinase BB isoenzyme, intestinal fatty acid binding protein
Contrast enema or colonoscopy for suspected colonic obstruction; ultrasound when radiation is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy)
redFlags: Fever, which raises concern for strangulation or systemic inflammation
Severe localized pain or peritoneal signs, suspicious for strangulated or closed-loop obstruction
Leukocytosis with immature forms plus metabolic acidosis, worrisome for ischemic necrosis and sepsis
Cecal diameter exceeding 10-12 cm in distal colonic obstruction with a competent ileocecal valve (impending ischemic perforation)
Free intraperitoneal air in a patient who has not recently had surgery (perforation)
Oliguria, hypotension, and tachycardia indicating severe intravascular volume depletion
harrison.prognosis: Overall morbidity and mortality appear to be decreasing. The mortality rate for patients with strangulation operated on within 24-30 h of symptom onset is about 8% but roughly triples thereafter. Most postoperative adhesive obstructions are partial and resolve spontaneously, and about 60-80% of selected mechanical obstructions can be managed conservatively; recurrence requiring readmission within 10 years occurs in ~20% of conservatively treated and 5-30% of operatively managed patients. Major complications after operation occur in roughly 12-47%, with higher risk for resection therapies and for patients with ASA class III or higher (Harrison 22e p.2589, 2593).
pitfalls: Barium should never be given orally until obstruction is excluded; in significant obstruction it may form concretions and renders later cross-sectional imaging or angiography uninterpretable (Harrison 22e p.2592-2593).
No laboratory test reliably distinguishes simple from strangulated obstruction; reliance on labs may delay needed intervention (Harrison 22e p.2592).
Bowel sounds are notoriously unreliable for diagnosis, and pain may be out of proportion to physical findings, masking strangulation or mimicking mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591).
Distal colonic obstruction with an incompetent ileocecal valve can present late and mimic distal small-bowel obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2591).
Imaging intervention should not be delayed when signs strongly suggest high-grade/complete obstruction or bowel compromise (Harrison 22e p.2592).
harrison.severityClassification: Mechanical obstruction is graded as partial, high grade, or complete, correlating with complication risk and urgency. It is further classified as simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia supervene, and closed-loop when both ends of a segment are occluded (highest risk of strangulation) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).
management: Nasogastric decompression, bowel rest, and intravenous fluid and electrolyte correction as initial conservative management
Water-soluble oral contrast for adhesive small-bowel obstruction, which is both prognostic and can promote resolution
Prompt surgical intervention for complete, closed-loop, or strangulated obstruction and for obstructing hernias
Adhesiolysis or bowel resection with treatment of the underlying cause at operation
Analgesia and antiemetics with correction of metabolic derangement
Serial clinical and biochemical monitoring for signs of ischaemia or strangulation prompting urgent surgery
Endoscopic stenting or decompression for selected malignant or non-strangulating colonic obstruction
